newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OPEC set to let winter mop up Iraqi oil.
newsitem.headline: OPEC set to let winter mop up Iraqi oil.

text.p: OPEC at talks opening in Vienna on Wednesday is set to extend current oil output quotas into 1997 and trust that avid consumer demand for winter fuel will mop up any resumed Iraqi exports and keep prices firm.

Several ministers said they hoped the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries would just roll over current quotas, following progress at the United Nations towards finally easing the 1990 Gulf War ban on sales by Iraq.
"It will be a rollover. I can tell you 99 percent that is the case," a Gulf source said.
The source also said that OPEC linchpin Saudi Arabia and Gulf allies Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates believe that oil demand is strong enough to absorb Iraqi sales if these materialise.
"The market is very healthy. Demand is strong. Stocks are low. And winter has just started," the source said, giving an insight into Saudi views ahead of Wednesday's talks.
The present quota accord, likely to be extended until at least June 30, was reached six months ago and wrote in an extra 800,000 barrels daily of exports to come from Iraq.

These exports have yet to begin, but in the latest New York talks the Iraqis say they have accepted U.N. conditions that had delayed implementation of an accord for them to sell oil worth $2 billion to buy food and medicine,

Violations of mandated quotas are said by Western monitors to have already lifted actual OPEC production, even without any Iraqi sales yet, by as much as a million barrels daily above the agreed ceiling of 25.03 million.
But the Saudis and other key OPEC nations seem to feel that, vexing as the violations may be, the market can absorb more oil.

Snow greeted the ministers as they flew in to Vienna on Tuesday. It was a reminder that oil companies are frantically trying to rebuild very low stocks of heating fuel ahead of what looks so far like being a harsh northern winter.
"Demand is whatever OPEC is producing," the Gulf source said. "We will definitely end this year with the lowest stocks in 20 years".
The benchmark Brent Blend of crude dropped some 40 cents on Monday on news from New York that Iraq now accepted conditions the food-for-peace deal.
But Brent stabilised on Tuesday at $22.75 per barrel, not too far off the recent post-Gulf War highs to which it was driven by the scramble to fill depleted stocks.
The price compares with $18 when OPEC met in June.
Independent analysts also agree that the market is unlikely to collapse, although they predict that Iraqi sales plus OPEC quota violations may mean some erosion of prices in 1997.
"The market is tight and it can take anything that is thrown at it right now," said Geoff Pyne, an energy economist with UBS Limited in London.
"But if Iraq returns soon it could be that prices will soften more quickly in the spring than we had expected."
With Iraq selling again, Pyne predicts an average 1997 price for Brent Blend at around $18.50 per barrel.

Iran's oil minister, Gholamreza Aqazadeh, told reporters on Tuesday after a session of OPEC's own quota compliance committee that members who are alleged to be exceeding their quotas have mostly denied any infringement.
Just one member, Venezuela, is alone alleged to be in excess by 800,000 barrels, or as much as OPEC allocated Iraq.
